cueCard.title: Describe a teacher who had a strong influence on you.
points: what subject he or she taught you
what was special about his or her teaching
cueCard.final: and explain how this teacher influenced you.

sample:
I'd like to talk about Mr Zhou, who was my English teacher in my last two years of high school. He was in his fifties, quite short, and always wore the same grey jacket, so at first we didn't expect much from him. But he turned out to be one of the best teachers I've ever had.

What made him special was the way he taught. Instead of making us memorise long lists of words, he'd bring in English songs, short news clips and even comic strips, and we'd work out the meaning together. He also had this habit of writing one interesting sentence on the board every morning, and whoever could explain the grammar behind it got a small prize, usually a sweet. It sounds silly, but we all competed like crazy.

The thing I remember most, though, is how patient he was. I was really shy back then, and my spoken English was terrible. Rather than putting me on the spot in class, he used to chat with me for a few minutes after lessons, just about films or football. Gradually I stopped being afraid of making mistakes.

As for how he influenced me, I'd say he changed my whole attitude towards learning. Before his class, English was just a subject I had to pass. After it, it became something I genuinely enjoyed. In fact, I don't think I'd be preparing for IELTS now if it weren't for him. We still send each other messages on Teachers' Day, and he always asks how my English is going.

part3.q: What qualities make a good teacher?
part3.sample: I think patience is probably the most important quality, because students learn at very different speeds, and a teacher who gets frustrated easily can make weaker students give up. Good teachers also need to be able to explain difficult ideas in simple language. For example, my best maths teacher used everyday situations, like splitting a restaurant bill, to explain percentages. Finally, I'd say enthusiasm matters a lot. If the teacher clearly loves the subject, students tend to pick up that energy.

part3.q: Do you think teachers are as respected today as they were in the past?
part3.sample: In China, teachers are still generally respected, but I think the relationship has changed. In the past, a teacher's word was almost law, and parents rarely questioned them. Nowadays parents are better educated and have more access to information, so they're more likely to challenge a teacher's decisions, sometimes in parent group chats. In a way, that's healthy, because it keeps schools accountable. But it also puts a lot of pressure on teachers, and some of them feel undervalued as a result.

part3.q: Will online learning replace teachers in classrooms in the future?
part3.sample: I don't think it will replace them completely. Online courses are great for delivering information, and they let people learn anywhere at their own pace. But a big part of a teacher's job isn't just passing on knowledge. It's motivating students, noticing when someone is struggling and helping children develop social skills. A video can't really do that. What I expect is a blended model, where students learn basic content online and then use class time for discussion and practice.

part3.q: Is it better for students to have strict teachers or relaxed ones?
part3.sample: I'd say it depends on the age of the students. Younger children usually need clear rules and a bit of strictness, otherwise classes can get chaotic and nobody learns much. With teenagers and adults, though, a more relaxed style often works better, because it encourages them to ask questions and share their opinions. Ideally, a teacher should be firm about things like deadlines and behaviour, but friendly and approachable at the same time. My favourite teachers managed to strike that balance.

cueCard.title: Describe a person you know who is good at solving problems.
points: how you know him or her
what problems you have seen him or her solve
cueCard.final: and explain why you think this person is good at solving problems.

sample:
The person I'm going to describe is my cousin Lin, who's a couple of years older than me and works as an engineer for a company that makes water pumps. We grew up in the same neighbourhood, so we've always been really close, more like siblings than cousins.

Lin is the person everyone in our family calls when something goes wrong. If the Wi-Fi stops working, if my aunt's washing machine starts leaking, or even if someone needs advice about a difficult boss, she's the first one we turn to. One example that really sticks in my mind happened a couple of years ago, when my grandparents' flat kept flooding every time it rained heavily. Two different repair companies came and couldn't find the cause. Lin spent a whole weekend there, going floor by floor, and she eventually worked out that a pipe on the balcony above was blocked with leaves. Once it was cleared, the problem disappeared.

So why is she so good at it? I think there are a few reasons. First of all, she stays calm. While the rest of us are panicking, she's asking questions and writing things down. Secondly, she's incredibly patient. She'll try one possible solution, check whether it works, and then move on to the next, without getting frustrated. And finally, she's not afraid to admit when she doesn't know something. She'll happily watch a video or ask an expert.

To be honest, I've learned a lot from watching her, especially that most problems look much smaller once you break them down.

part3.q: Why are some people better at solving problems than others?
part3.sample: I think part of it is personality. Some people are naturally calm and curious, so they enjoy figuring things out rather than feeling stressed. But I believe experience plays an even bigger role. Someone who has faced lots of challenges, maybe because they had to look after themselves from a young age, builds up a kind of toolkit of strategies. Education matters too. People who were encouraged to ask why at school tend to approach problems more logically than those who just memorised answers.

part3.q: Should schools teach problem-solving skills as a separate subject?
part3.sample: I'm not sure it needs to be a separate subject, but it should definitely get more attention. Personally, I think it works better when it's built into existing subjects. For instance, in science classes students could design their own experiments instead of just following instructions, and in maths they could tackle real-life problems like planning a budget. That way, they'd see that problem-solving is useful everywhere, not just something you study for one hour a week.

part3.q: Do you think people rely too much on technology to solve their problems?
part3.sample: To some extent, yes. These days, the first reaction to almost any problem is to search online or ask an app, and that's often helpful. The danger is that people stop thinking for themselves. I've seen friends who can't find their way around their own city without a map app, for example. On the other hand, technology lets ordinary people fix things they'd never have managed before, like repairing a bike by following a video. So it's really about using it wisely.

part3.q: Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?
part3.sample: It really depends on the problem. For something simple or personal, working alone is usually faster, because you don't need to spend time discussing every step. But for complex problems, like designing a new product or organising a big event, teams tend to do much better. Different people notice different things, and someone else might spot a mistake you completely missed. The downside is that teams can waste time arguing, so they need a clear leader to keep things moving.

cueCard.title: Describe an older person you admire.
points: how you know him or her
what he or she is like
cueCard.final: and explain why you admire this person.

sample:
I'd like to talk about my grandmother on my mother's side. She's eighty-two now and still lives on her own in a small town about an hour from my parents' place. I spent most of my summer holidays with her when I was a child, so we've always had a special bond.

She's quite a small woman, but she has an amazing amount of energy. She gets up at five every morning, does tai chi in the square with her friends, and then spends hours in her vegetable garden. She's also incredibly sociable. Whenever I visit, there's always a neighbour popping in to drop off some dumplings or ask her opinion about something. She seems to know everyone in town.

What I admire most about her is her attitude to life. She grew up in a very poor family and had to leave school at twelve to look after her younger brothers. Despite that, she taught herself to read in her twenties, and in her seventies she even learned to use a smartphone so she could video-call her grandchildren. She never complains about the hardships she went through. Instead, she always says that every difficult period taught her something.

I think she's the reason I try not to give up when things get tough. Whenever I feel stressed about work or exams, I remind myself of everything she's dealt with, and suddenly my problems don't seem so serious. I really hope I'll be as positive and curious as she is when I'm her age.

part3.q: What can young people learn from older people?
part3.sample: Quite a lot, I think. Older people have lived through situations that young people have only read about, so they can offer a sense of perspective. For example, my grandparents experienced real hardship, and listening to them makes me appreciate how comfortable my life is. They also tend to have practical skills that are disappearing, like growing vegetables or repairing clothes. Perhaps most importantly, they've learned the hard way what really matters in life, which is usually family and health rather than money.

part3.q: Is it better for elderly people to live with their families or in care homes?
part3.sample: Traditionally in China, older people lived with their children, and many still prefer that, because they feel looked after and less lonely. However, it isn't always practical. When both adult children work long hours, an elderly parent might end up alone at home all day anyway. In those cases, a good care home with trained staff and social activities could actually offer a better quality of life. I think the key is that the decision should be made together, not forced on the older person.

part3.q: How will an ageing population affect society in the future?
part3.sample: It's likely to have a huge impact. With fewer young people working and more people retired, governments will face rising costs for pensions and healthcare, which could mean higher taxes. There may also be a shortage of carers and nurses. On the positive side, it could create new industries, such as products and services designed for older consumers. Some countries are already experimenting with robots in care homes, so technology may help fill part of the gap.

part3.q: Do you think older people should keep working after retirement age?
part3.sample: If they want to and they're healthy enough, I think it can be really good for them. Work gives people a sense of purpose and keeps their minds active, and they can pass on valuable experience to younger colleagues. My neighbour, for instance, retired as a doctor but still volunteers at a clinic twice a week, and she seems happier than ever. That said, nobody should be forced to keep working just because their pension is too small to live on.

cueCard.title: Describe a quiet place you like to go to.
points: how you found out about it
cueCard.final: and explain why you like spending time there.

sample:
The place I'd like to describe is a small tea house hidden in an old lane in the centre of my city. It's only about ten minutes' walk from a really busy shopping street, but once you step inside, the noise just disappears.

I actually found it by accident. About two years ago, I was walking around on a rainy Sunday afternoon and needed somewhere to shelter. I noticed a wooden sign with a single Chinese character on it, pushed open the door, and found myself in this peaceful courtyard with a few tables, some bamboo and a tiny fish pond. The owner is a retired music teacher, and she plays soft traditional music in the background.

These days I go there two or three times a month, usually on a weekend morning. I order a pot of green tea, which is refilled for free, and I just sit for a couple of hours. Sometimes I read a novel, sometimes I write in my journal, and sometimes I do nothing at all and just watch the fish. There's no Wi-Fi, which I thought would be annoying at first, but it's actually the best thing about it.

The reason I love it so much is that it gives me a break from my busy, noisy life. My job involves constant meetings and messages, and my flat is on a main road, so real silence is pretty rare for me. In that tea house, I can finally hear my own thoughts. I always leave feeling calmer and more creative, as if someone has pressed a reset button in my head.

part3.q: Why do some people find it hard to find quiet places in cities?
part3.sample: Mainly because cities are so densely populated. There's constant traffic, construction work and people everywhere, and space is so expensive that very little of it is left empty. Even parks can be noisy, with people dancing or playing music. On top of that, many people now carry noise around with them, in the form of phones and notifications. So even if you find a physically quiet spot, it's hard to feel truly peaceful unless you switch your devices off.

part3.q: Do you think noise pollution is a serious problem?
part3.sample: Yes, I think it's more serious than most people realise. Unlike air pollution, you can't see it, so it often gets ignored. But research suggests that long-term exposure to traffic noise can disturb sleep and raise stress levels, and it may even contribute to heart problems. In my own neighbourhood, there was a period when a building site worked late into the night, and lots of residents complained of headaches. I think cities should enforce stricter rules on working hours and use better sound barriers.

part3.q: Are young people and older people different in how they like to relax?
part3.sample: Generally, yes, although it's a bit of a stereotype. Older people often prefer calm, sociable activities, like chatting in the park, playing chess or doing gentle exercise. Young people, by contrast, tend to relax in more active or digital ways, such as gaming, going to the gym or scrolling through social media. But I think the gap is getting smaller. Lots of young people I know are getting into things like fishing and tea, partly as a reaction against their stressful, screen-heavy lives.

part3.q: Should governments create more public quiet spaces?
part3.sample: I think they should, especially in crowded cities. Not everyone can afford to escape to the countryside at weekends, so public spaces like libraries, gardens and reading rooms give ordinary people a chance to rest and recharge. Some cities have started turning unused rooftops into small gardens, which seems like a clever idea that doesn't cost much. In the long run, investing in these places could even save money, because people who manage stress better are less likely to need medical treatment.

cueCard.title: Describe a city you visited that impressed you.
points: when and why you went there
cueCard.final: and explain what impressed you about this city.

sample:
The city I'd like to talk about is Xi'an, in the north-west of China. I went there about three years ago with two friends from university, just after we'd graduated. We wanted one last trip together before we all started work, and since we were all interested in history, Xi'an seemed like the perfect choice.

We stayed for four days, and we tried to pack in as much as possible. On the first day, we went to see the Terracotta Warriors, which are about an hour outside the city. I'd seen photos of them many times, but standing in front of thousands of life-sized soldiers, each with a different face, was something else entirely. We also hired bikes and cycled all the way around the old city wall, which took a couple of hours. And every evening we ended up in the Muslim Quarter, eating our way through the street food stalls. The lamb soup with torn-up bread was my favourite.

What impressed me most was the way the ancient and the modern sit side by side. You can be standing on a wall that's hundreds of years old, and right below you there are metro stations, shopping malls and people delivering takeaways on electric scooters. Somehow it doesn't feel strange, though. The history feels like part of everyday life rather than something locked away in a museum.

I was also struck by how friendly people were. A shop owner spent ages giving us tips on where to eat, without trying to sell us anything. I'd love to go back one day and spend more time exploring.

part3.q: What makes a city attractive to tourists?
part3.sample: I think there are a few key things. History and culture are obviously a big draw, because people want to see things they can't see at home, like ancient buildings or traditional festivals. Food is another huge factor, especially for Chinese tourists, who often plan whole trips around local dishes. But practical things matter too. If a city has good public transport, clear signs in several languages and reasonably priced hotels, visitors are much more likely to recommend it to others.

part3.q: Does tourism bring more benefits or problems to local people?
part3.sample: On balance, I'd say it brings more benefits, mainly economic ones. Tourism creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and shops, and it can bring money into areas that would otherwise struggle. However, the problems can be serious if it isn't managed well. In some popular cities, rents have shot up because so many flats are rented to tourists, and locals end up being pushed out. Crowds can also damage historic sites. So I think limits on visitor numbers are sometimes necessary.

part3.q: Should old buildings in cities be protected or replaced with modern ones?
part3.sample: I believe the most important historic buildings should definitely be protected, because once they're gone, they're gone forever, and they give a city its identity. That said, we can't keep every old building, especially if it's unsafe or the city desperately needs housing. A good compromise is to renovate old buildings for new uses. In my city, for example, an old textile factory was turned into an arts centre with cafes and studios, and it's now one of the liveliest areas in town.

part3.q: How do you think cities will change in the next twenty years?
part3.sample: I expect cities to become greener and smarter. Many governments are already planting more trees and building cycle lanes to cope with rising temperatures and pollution, and I think that trend will speed up. Technology will probably play a bigger role too, with things like driverless buses and sensors that control traffic lights automatically. One concern, though, is cost. If cities become too expensive, ordinary workers may have to move further out, so planners will need to make sure housing stays affordable.

cueCard.title: Describe a park or garden in your city.
cueCard.final: and explain how you feel about this place.

sample:
I'm going to talk about Riverside Park, which runs along the river on the east side of my city. It's quite a long, narrow park, maybe three kilometres from end to end, and it's only a five-minute walk from my flat, so I go there all the time.

The park was built about ten years ago on what used to be an old dockyard, and the designers kept some of the original features, like a couple of rusty cranes, which now look like giant sculptures. There's a wide path for walking and cycling right along the water, lots of willow trees, a small lake with lotus flowers in summer, and a few open lawns where people can have picnics. At night the bridges over the river are lit up, so it looks really beautiful.

What I love is how many different things people do there. Early in the morning, you see older people doing tai chi or practising calligraphy on the ground with water and giant brushes. During the day, parents bring their kids to the playground, and at weekends the lawns are full of young people flying kites or playing frisbee. In the evening, groups of women do square dancing to loud music, which can be a bit noisy, but it's quite fun to watch.

For me, the park is somewhere to unwind. After a long day at work, I often go for a jog or just a slow walk by the water, and it helps me clear my head. I think it's made the whole neighbourhood feel more like a community, and I'd really miss it if I moved away.

part3.q: Why are parks important in cities?
part3.sample: Parks are sometimes called the lungs of a city, and I think that's a good description. Trees help clean the air and keep temperatures down in summer, which is increasingly important as cities get hotter. But parks have social benefits too. They're one of the few places where people of all ages and incomes can spend time for free. Children can play safely, older people can meet their friends, and office workers can take a break from staring at screens.

part3.q: Who should pay for public parks, the government or private companies?
part3.sample: I think the main responsibility should lie with the government, because parks are a public good that everyone should be able to enjoy. If private companies paid for everything, there's a risk they'd start charging entrance fees or filling parks with advertising. That said, I don't see a problem with companies sponsoring things like benches, playgrounds or flower beds, as long as the park stays free and open to all. That kind of partnership can reduce the burden on taxpayers.

part3.q: Do people spend less time outdoors than they used to?
part3.sample: I think so, especially children. When my parents were young, kids played outside until dinner time almost every day. Now children spend much more time indoors, partly because of homework and partly because of screens. Parents also worry more about safety and traffic. Adults are similar. Many of us go from our flat to the car or metro, then to an office, and back again, without spending much time in fresh air. Interestingly, outdoor sports have become fashionable, but they're often organised activities rather than casual play.

part3.q: How could parks be designed to attract more young people?
part3.sample: I think designers need to think beyond flowers and benches. Young people tend to like spaces where they can be active or social, so things like skate parks, outdoor fitness equipment and basketball courts would definitely help. Free Wi-Fi and phone charging points might sound strange in a park, but they'd encourage people to stay longer. Some parks near me also host weekend markets and outdoor film screenings, and those always attract a young crowd. Basically, parks need to offer something to do, not just something to look at.

cueCard.title: Describe a gift you received that was important to you.
cueCard.final: and explain why it is important to you.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a watch that my parents gave me when I left home to go to university. It's nothing fancy, just a simple silver watch with a black leather strap and a plain white face, but it's probably the most meaningful thing I own.

I remember the moment really clearly. It was the night before I took the train to university, which was more than a thousand kilometres away. We'd just finished dinner, and my dad, who isn't very good at expressing his feelings, suddenly put a small box on the table and pushed it towards me without saying a word. My mum explained that they'd chosen it together and had the date engraved on the back. I found out later that it cost almost a month of my dad's salary at the time, which really shocked me, because they were always very careful with money.

The reason it matters so much to me is that it represents the moment I started to become independent. Whenever I look at it, I remember how nervous I felt leaving home, and also how much my parents believed in me. During my first year, when I felt homesick or stressed before exams, I'd look at the engraving on the back and it would calm me down a bit.

I don't wear it every day now, because the strap is getting worn and I'm worried about damaging it. But I always put it on for important occasions, like job interviews. It sounds a bit superstitious, but it feels like it brings me luck.

part3.q: Why do people give gifts?
part3.sample: There are lots of reasons. The most obvious one is to show love or appreciation, for example on birthdays or when someone has helped you. But gifts also have a social function. In China, people often bring a gift when they visit someone's home for the first time, and it's a way of showing respect and good manners. In business, gifts can help build relationships, although companies now have strict rules about that to avoid any suggestion of bribery.

part3.q: Is the price of a gift important?
part3.sample: It shouldn't be, but in reality, it sometimes is. In certain situations, like weddings, people do pay attention to how much money is in the red envelope, because it's seen as a sign of how close the relationship is. However, I think the gifts people remember most are usually the thoughtful ones. A handwritten letter or a photo album can mean far more than something expensive, because it shows that the giver really thought about you and spent time on it.

part3.q: Do you think people put too much emphasis on material things nowadays?
part3.sample: Yes, I think many people do, and social media is partly to blame. When you constantly see influencers showing off designer bags and new cars, it's easy to start believing that happiness comes from owning things. Advertising also creates needs that we didn't have before. Having said that, I've noticed a growing movement, especially among young people, towards minimalism, where people try to own less and spend more on experiences like travel or learning a skill. So attitudes may be slowly shifting.

part3.q: How has the way people give gifts changed in recent years?
part3.sample: It's changed quite a lot because of technology. These days, you can send someone a digital red envelope or a gift card through an app in seconds, even if they live on the other side of the country. Online shopping also means people can have presents delivered directly. It's very convenient, but I feel something has been lost. Wrapping a present and handing it over in person makes the moment more personal, so I still try to do that for my closest friends and family.

cueCard.title: Describe a piece of technology, other than a phone, that you find useful.
points: when and how you got it
cueCard.final: and explain why you find it useful.

sample:
The piece of technology I'd like to describe is a pair of noise-cancelling headphones. They're the over-ear type, dark grey, and they fold up into a small case, so I can carry them in my bag wherever I go.

I bought them about eighteen months ago, shortly after my company moved to a new open-plan office. I'd been finding it really hard to concentrate there, because there were always people on the phone or chatting nearby. A colleague recommended this particular model, and although it was quite pricey, I decided it was worth investing in. I waited for an online sale and saved around thirty per cent, which made me feel a bit better about spending so much.

Honestly, I use them every single day. In the morning, I wear them on the metro, which is incredibly noisy, and they turn the roar of the train into a quiet hum. At work, I put them on whenever I need to focus on a report. And in the evenings, I use them for my IELTS listening practice, because they make the recordings much clearer and I don't miss small words like articles and prepositions.

The main reason I find them so useful is that they give me control over my environment. I can't change how noisy my city is, but with these, I can create my own little bubble of quiet whenever I need it. I've noticed that I'm less tired at the end of the day, too, probably because my brain isn't constantly processing background noise. They're easily one of the best things I've ever bought.

part3.q: What kinds of technology are most important in people's daily lives today?
part3.sample: Apart from smartphones, I'd say the internet itself is the most important, because so many services depend on it, from banking to booking a doctor's appointment. Mobile payment systems are also essential in China. Many people hardly carry cash at all anymore. And in homes, things like washing machines and rice cookers are so common that we forget they're technology at all. If they broke down, though, most of us would struggle to cope for even a few days.

part3.q: Do older people find it difficult to keep up with new technology?
part3.sample: Many do, yes, but I think it's often a lack of support rather than a lack of ability. Technology changes so quickly, and apps are usually designed with young users in mind, with tiny icons and complicated menus. My grandmother found it hard at first, but once I wrote down the steps for her, she picked it up quite quickly. It would help if companies offered simpler versions of their apps, and if communities ran free classes for older residents.

part3.q: Has technology made people less sociable?
part3.sample: In some ways, yes. You often see a group of friends sitting at a restaurant table, all looking at their phones instead of talking to each other, which is a bit sad. On the other hand, technology helps people stay in touch across long distances. I can video-call my family every week even though I live far away, and people with unusual hobbies can find like-minded communities online. So I'd say technology changes how we socialise, rather than simply making us less sociable.

part3.q: What new technology do you think will change our lives in the future?
part3.sample: I think artificial intelligence will have the biggest impact, and it's already happening. AI tools can now translate languages, write basic reports and help doctors spot diseases in medical scans. In the next decade, I expect them to become a normal part of most jobs. Self-driving cars are another possibility, although I suspect it'll take longer than people predict, because of safety laws. The big challenge will be helping workers whose jobs disappear to retrain for new roles.

cueCard.title: Describe something you own that you have kept for a long time.
cueCard.final: and explain why you have kept it for so long.

sample:
Something I've kept for a really long time is an old English-Chinese dictionary that I've had since I was about thirteen. It's a thick paperback, and by now it's in pretty bad shape. The cover is held together with tape, some pages are falling out, and the edges have turned yellow.

I got it when I started middle school. My English teacher told everyone to buy a proper dictionary, and my mum took me to the biggest bookshop in town to choose one. I remember feeling very grown-up, because it was the first time I'd been allowed to pick a book with my own pocket money, even though she paid for most of it in the end.

For years, I used it almost every day. Whenever I came across a new word, I'd look it up, underline it and write an example sentence in the margin. Some pages are completely covered in my handwriting, and there are even little drawings and notes from my classmates. Now it sits on the top shelf of the bookcase in my bedroom, right next to my IELTS books.

To be honest, I hardly ever open it these days, because I use dictionary apps on my phone. But I can't bring myself to throw it away. It's like a record of my whole journey with English. When I flip through it, I can see how my handwriting changed and which words I struggled with as a teenager. It also reminds me that progress comes from small daily efforts, which is a useful thing to remember while I'm preparing for this exam.

part3.q: Why do some people keep old things that they no longer use?
part3.sample: I think the main reason is emotional. Objects can hold memories, so throwing them away can feel like throwing away part of your past. My mother still has my baby clothes in a box, for example. Some people also keep things for practical reasons, thinking they might need them one day. This is especially common among older generations who grew up with very little and learned never to waste anything. For them, throwing away something that still works feels almost wrong.

part3.q: Do young people today value their possessions less than in the past?
part3.sample: Generally, I'd say yes. Because goods are cheaper and easier to buy than ever, people replace things much more quickly. When my parents were young, a bicycle or a radio was a big investment, so they looked after it carefully and repaired it when it broke. Today, if a phone is a couple of years old, many people just upgrade. However, young people often value experiences more than objects, so it's not that they care less, just that they care about different things.

part3.q: What problems are caused by people throwing things away too often?
part3.sample: The biggest problem is waste. Landfill sites are filling up, and a lot of electronic waste contains harmful chemicals that can leak into the soil and water. Producing new goods also uses huge amounts of energy and raw materials, which contributes to climate change. Fast fashion is a good example. Cheap clothes are often worn just a few times before being thrown away. I think we need better recycling systems, and companies should be encouraged to make products that last longer and are easier to repair.

part3.q: Do you think museums should keep everyday objects as well as valuable ones?
part3.sample: Yes, I think everyday objects are just as important. Valuable items like jewellery or paintings show us how the rich lived, but ordinary things, like cooking pots, school textbooks or old bus tickets, tell us about the lives of most people. I once visited a small museum that recreated a typical family flat from the 1980s, and it was fascinating, because my parents could point out things they actually used. Objects like that help younger generations understand recent history in a very personal way.

cueCard.title: Describe a celebration you enjoyed.
points: when and where it took place
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoyed it.

sample:
I'd like to talk about my grandparents' golden wedding anniversary, which we celebrated last October. These are my dad's parents, and they'd been married for exactly fifty years, so the whole family agreed it was a big deal and we needed to do something special.

The celebration took place in a restaurant in their hometown, a small town in the countryside. My aunt booked a private room big enough for about forty people, and my cousins and I spent the afternoon decorating it with red balloons, flowers and a huge banner. Almost all our relatives came, some of whom I hadn't seen for years, and a few of my grandparents' old friends from the factory where they used to work turned up as well.

The best part of the evening was a little surprise we'd prepared. Over the previous few months, we'd collected old photos from everyone in the family and turned them into a short slideshow, starting from my grandparents' wedding day in the 1970s. When it started playing, the whole room went quiet. My grandfather, who almost never shows his emotions, actually had tears in his eyes. After that, there was a lot of eating and toasting, and my grandmother sang a folk song she'd loved since she was young.

I think I enjoyed it so much because it felt really genuine. It wasn't about expensive gifts or showing off. It was simply a chance to celebrate two people who'd stuck together through some very hard times. It also made me appreciate how lucky I am to have such a close family.

part3.q: Why do people like to celebrate special occasions?
part3.sample: I think celebrations give structure and meaning to our lives. Everyday life can be quite repetitive, so marking special moments, like birthdays, weddings or graduations, helps us notice how far we've come. They also bring people together. In busy modern societies, family members often live in different cities, and a celebration gives everyone a reason to make the effort to meet. And of course, there's the simple fact that people enjoy good food, music and a break from routine.

part3.q: Are traditional festivals still important to young people?
part3.sample: I'd say they're still important, but young people celebrate them differently. For instance, during the Spring Festival, many young people still go home, but they might spend more time on their phones sending digital red envelopes than visiting neighbours. Some traditions, like making dumplings together, are still very popular, whereas others, like certain religious rituals, are fading. Interestingly, there's been a revival of interest in traditional culture recently. Lots of young people now wear traditional clothing at festivals and share photos online.

part3.q: Do you think celebrations have become too commercial?
part3.sample: In many cases, yes. Shops and online platforms now turn almost every festival into a shopping event, and the pressure to buy gifts and expensive decorations can be quite stressful. Even Valentine's Day has become more about buying flowers and chocolates at inflated prices than about the relationship itself. Weddings are another example. Some couples spend a fortune to impress their guests. That said, commercialisation isn't all bad. It supports many small businesses, and people can still choose to celebrate in a simple way.

part3.q: How might celebrations change in the future?
part3.sample: I think they'll become more digital and more personalised. We're already seeing virtual birthday parties and weddings that are live-streamed for relatives abroad, and that will probably become normal. There may also be fewer large, formal events. Many young couples, for example, prefer a small wedding with close friends rather than a huge banquet. Environmental concerns could change things too. Fireworks have already been restricted in many cities because of air pollution, and people may choose more eco-friendly ways to celebrate.

cueCard.title: Describe a sports event or competition you watched or took part in.
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about it.

sample:
I'm going to talk about a half marathon I ran in last spring. It was held in my city, and it was the first long-distance race I'd ever done. About ten thousand people took part, from serious athletes to complete beginners like me.

I'd signed up about four months before, mostly because a colleague dared me to. At that time, I could barely run five kilometres without stopping, so I followed an online training plan and ran three or four times a week, gradually increasing the distance. There were definitely mornings when I wanted to stay in bed, but having a fixed date to aim for kept me going.

On the day itself, the atmosphere was amazing. The race started at seven in the morning in front of the city stadium, and the route went along the river and through the old town. Local residents lined the streets, cheering and handing out water and slices of orange, and there were even a few bands playing music along the way. The first ten kilometres felt fine, but around the fifteen-kilometre mark my legs started to really ache, and I had to slow down and walk for a minute or two. Luckily, a stranger ran beside me for a while and kept telling me I was nearly there.

I finished in just under two and a half hours, which isn't fast at all, but I was incredibly proud of myself. I remember feeling exhausted and emotional at the same time. More than anything, it taught me that I'm capable of much more than I think, as long as I prepare properly.

part3.q: Why do people enjoy watching sports events?
part3.sample: I think it's mainly about the excitement and unpredictability. Unlike a film, nobody knows how a match will end, so there's real tension right up to the last minute. Watching sport is also a very social activity. People gather in bars or at friends' homes to watch big games, and supporting the same team creates a strong sense of belonging. For some fans, their team is almost part of their identity, and they've supported it since childhood.

part3.q: Is competition good for children?
part3.sample: In moderation, I think it's healthy. Competing teaches children to set goals, work hard and deal with disappointment, which are important skills for adult life. Losing a game, for example, can teach a child how to handle failure without giving up. However, when parents or schools put too much emphasis on winning, children can become anxious and start to see their classmates as rivals rather than friends. So the focus should be on personal improvement and teamwork, not just on coming first.

part3.q: Should governments spend money on hosting international sports events?
part3.sample: It's a difficult question. Hosting something like the Olympics can boost national pride, attract tourists and lead to better infrastructure, such as new metro lines and sports facilities. However, the costs are enormous, and some host cities have been left with huge debts and stadiums that are hardly used afterwards. Personally, I think it only makes sense if the government plans carefully for long-term use. Otherwise, the money might be better spent on local sports facilities that ordinary people can use every day.

part3.q: Why are professional athletes paid so much money?
part3.sample: Mainly because they generate enormous amounts of money for others. Top athletes attract millions of viewers, which means TV companies and sponsors are willing to pay huge sums to be associated with them. Their careers are also very short, often finished by their mid-thirties, and they risk serious injuries. Even so, I sometimes feel the salaries are out of proportion. It seems unfair that a footballer can earn more in a week than a nurse earns in several years.

cueCard.title: Describe a public event held in your city that you attended.
points: when and where it was held
cueCard.final: and explain whether you would like to go again.

sample:
I'd like to describe the lantern fair that's held in my city every year at the Lantern Festival, which marks the end of the Chinese New Year celebrations. I went this year with my parents and my younger cousin, and it was the first time I'd been in about five years.

The fair takes place in the old town, around a big square and along the streets leading down to the river. For about a week, the whole area is decorated with thousands of lanterns. Some are traditional red ones, but there are also huge displays, some taller than a house, in the shapes of dragons, rabbits and even famous local buildings. This year, a lot of them had moving parts and changing lights, which made them look almost alive.

There's plenty to do apart from just looking at the lanterns. People walk around eating snacks from food stalls, especially tangyuan, the sweet rice balls that are traditionally eaten on that day. There's also a lantern riddle area, where riddles are written on little cards hanging under the lanterns, and if you guess one correctly, you can win a small prize. My cousin and I spent ages there and managed to solve three, which we were very pleased about.

Would I go again? Definitely, but I'd go a few days earlier next time. We went on the actual night of the festival, and it was unbelievably crowded. At some points we could hardly move, and it took nearly an hour to get out of the area. Still, seeing the river lit up with lanterns was so beautiful that it was worth it.

part3.q: Why are public festivals important for a city?
part3.sample: I think they help create a sense of community. In big cities, people often don't even know their neighbours, but at a festival, strangers chat, share food and enjoy the same experience together. Festivals also help keep local culture alive, by passing on traditions like lantern-making or folk music to younger generations. And of course, there's an economic benefit. A well-known festival can attract thousands of visitors, which is great for local restaurants, hotels and shops.

part3.q: What problems can large public events cause?
part3.sample: The most obvious one is overcrowding, which can actually be dangerous if the organisers don't control the number of people properly. There are also problems with traffic, noise and litter. After a big event, streets can be covered in rubbish, and local residents have to put up with the mess. In addition, security costs a lot of money, and that's usually paid for by taxpayers. To reduce these problems, many cities now require people to book free tickets online in advance, which helps manage numbers.

part3.q: Should traditional festivals change to attract more young people?
part3.sample: I think some change is natural and even necessary. If festivals stay exactly the same, younger people might see them as old-fashioned and lose interest. Adding modern elements, like light shows, music performances or interactive games, can make them more appealing. However, it's important not to lose the core meaning. If a traditional festival turns into just another shopping event, it loses what made it special in the first place. So the best approach is probably to update the format while keeping the traditions at the centre.

part3.q: Do you think international festivals like Halloween are becoming more popular in your country?
part3.sample: Yes, definitely, especially among young people in big cities. Halloween parties are now quite common in bars and shopping malls, and international schools celebrate it too. I think it's mainly because these festivals are seen as fun and fashionable, and social media spreads the images very quickly. Businesses also promote them heavily, because they're another chance to sell things. Some people worry that this threatens Chinese traditions, but I don't really agree. Most young people simply enjoy both and treat foreign festivals as an extra excuse to have fun.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when you helped someone.
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about helping this person.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a time last summer when I helped a tourist who was completely lost. It happened on a Saturday afternoon at the main railway station in my city. I was waiting for a friend, and I noticed a woman, probably in her sixties, standing near the ticket machines and looking really stressed.

She was from Germany, and she was travelling alone around China for the first time. Her phone had run out of battery, so she couldn't use her translation app or show anyone her booking, and the station staff she'd asked didn't speak much English. Her train was due to leave in less than an hour, and she couldn't even remember which of the city's two stations it was leaving from.

I went over and asked if she needed help, in my rather nervous English. First, I lent her my power bank so she could charge her phone. Once it came back on, we found her booking, and it turned out her train was actually leaving from the other station, about twenty minutes away. So I helped her get a taxi, explained the address to the driver and wrote it down in Chinese for her, just in case. She was so relieved that she gave me a big hug, which I wasn't expecting at all.

I felt really good afterwards, partly because I'd helped someone, but also because I'd actually used my English in a real situation and it worked. It gave my confidence a huge boost. She even sent me a message that evening to say she'd made it, and we've kept in touch since.

part3.q: Why do some people like to help others?
part3.sample: I think for most people, it simply feels good. Helping someone gives you a sense of satisfaction and makes you feel useful. Some people are also influenced by how they were raised. If your parents regularly helped neighbours or volunteered, you're more likely to see it as normal. And there's a practical side, too. In close communities, people help each other because they know they might need help themselves one day. It's a kind of unwritten agreement that makes society work better.

part3.q: Are people less willing to help strangers than they were in the past?
part3.sample: In some ways, maybe. In big cities, people are busy and often wary of strangers, partly because of news stories about scams, and some worry they might get into trouble if they try to help. But I don't think people are less kind. If you look online, there are countless examples of strangers raising money for someone who's ill or volunteering after natural disasters. So I'd say people are still willing to help, but they're more cautious about how they do it.

part3.q: Should schools require students to do volunteer work?
part3.sample: I think it's a good idea in principle, because volunteering teaches young people about responsibility and lets them see parts of society they'd never normally encounter. Spending an afternoon at a care home, for example, can really change a teenager's attitude towards older people. The risk is that if it's compulsory, students might just do the minimum to tick a box. Schools should therefore offer a wide range of options, so that students can find something they genuinely care about.

part3.q: Who should be responsible for helping people in need, the government or individuals?
part3.sample: I'd say both have a role, but the government should carry the main responsibility. Only governments have the resources to provide things like healthcare, housing support and pensions on a large scale, and they can make sure help is distributed fairly. Individuals and charities, however, can respond more quickly and personally. For example, when a family in my neighbourhood lost their home in a fire, neighbours collected clothes and money within a day, long before any official help arrived. Ideally, the two should work together.

cueCard.title: Describe a time when your plans changed unexpectedly.
points: what you had planned to do
cueCard.final: and explain how you felt about the change.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a holiday two years ago that didn't go the way I'd planned at all. My two best friends and I had booked a five-day trip to a small island off the south coast for the National Day holiday. We'd been planning it for months, and we were really looking forward to lying on the beach and eating seafood.

The day before we were due to leave, a typhoon suddenly changed direction and headed straight for the island. All the ferries were cancelled, and the local government advised tourists not to travel. At first, we were really disappointed, especially because we'd already paid for our hotel. Fortunately, the hotel gave us a full refund because of the weather warning.

So instead of giving up on the holiday completely, we sat down in a cafe, looked at a map, and picked somewhere we'd never considered before, a mountain town about three hours inland by train. We booked a small guesthouse that evening and set off the next morning. The town turned out to be absolutely charming. It had narrow stone streets, tea plantations on the hillsides and hardly any tourists. We spent our days hiking and chatting with locals, and we even learned how to pick and roast tea leaves at a family farm.

Looking back, I'm actually glad our plans changed. I'd been a bit of a control freak about travel before, always planning every detail. That trip taught me to be more flexible and open to surprises. Funnily enough, my friends and I still say it was one of the best holidays we've ever had.

part3.q: Is it important to make plans for the future?
part3.sample: I think so, because without plans, it's easy to drift along without achieving much. Having clear goals, like saving for a flat or passing an exam by a certain date, helps you prioritise and stay motivated. My IELTS preparation is a good example. Having a weekly schedule makes a huge difference. However, plans shouldn't be too rigid. Life is unpredictable, and people who can't adapt when things change often end up feeling frustrated. So I'd say it's important to plan, but also to review and adjust those plans regularly.

part3.q: Why do some people find it hard to deal with change?
part3.sample: I think change creates uncertainty, and many people find uncertainty stressful. When you're used to a routine, you know what to expect, and that makes you feel safe. A big change, like moving to a new city or starting a new job, forces you to learn new things and maybe fail in front of others. Personality also plays a part. Some people naturally enjoy novelty, while others prefer stability. Age can matter too, since older people may have more to lose if things go wrong.

part3.q: Do you think young people today plan their careers more carefully than in the past?
part3.sample: In a way, they have to. In my parents' generation, many people got a job after school and stayed in the same workplace for life, so there wasn't much to plan. Now the job market is far more competitive and changes quickly, so young people think carefully about which skills will be in demand. Many do internships early or take online courses on the side. At the same time, more young people are changing careers several times, so long-term plans are often less fixed than before.

part3.q: How can technology help people when their plans change suddenly?
part3.sample: Technology has made it much easier to adapt. If a flight is cancelled, for example, you can rebook it on an app within minutes, instead of queuing at a counter for hours. Map apps can find alternative routes when there's a traffic jam, and you can find a last-minute hotel or restaurant almost anywhere. Communication is easier too. You can instantly let people know you're running late. The downside, perhaps, is that we've become so dependent on these tools that we panic when our phone battery dies.

cueCard.title: Describe a book you enjoyed reading.
cueCard.final: and explain why you enjoyed it.

sample:
The book I'd like to talk about is The Old Man and the Sea by Ernest Hemingway. I first read it in Chinese at secondary school, but last year I decided to try it in English as part of my IELTS preparation, and it turned out to be the perfect choice.

It's a very short novel, only around a hundred pages, which is one reason I picked it. The story is pretty simple. It's about an old Cuban fisherman called Santiago, who hasn't caught a fish for eighty-four days, and the other fishermen think he's finished. One day he sails far out to sea alone and hooks an enormous marlin. For nearly three days, he struggles with the fish, even though he's exhausted and his hands are badly cut. He finally kills it and ties it to the side of his boat, but on the way home, sharks attack and eat almost all of it. By the time he gets back to shore, there's nothing left but the skeleton.

I enjoyed it for a few reasons. First, the language is surprisingly simple. Hemingway uses short sentences and everyday words, so I could follow most of it without a dictionary, which was really encouraging. But more importantly, the story made me think. On the surface, Santiago loses everything, but he never gives up, and he keeps his dignity right to the end.

I read it during a period when I was feeling frustrated with my slow progress in English, and the old man's determination really inspired me. It reminded me that what matters is how hard you try, not just the result.

part3.q: Do young people read less than they used to?
part3.sample: It depends on what you mean by reading. Young people probably read fewer printed books than previous generations did, mainly because there are so many other forms of entertainment competing for their attention. But they actually read a lot every day, just in different forms, like online articles, social media posts and web novels. The concern is that most of this is quick, shallow reading. Fewer young people seem to have the patience for long, complex texts, and that's a skill that needs practice.

part3.q: What are the benefits of reading for children?
part3.sample: There are huge benefits. The most obvious one is language development. Children who read regularly pick up a much wider vocabulary and usually become better writers. Reading also improves concentration, because you have to follow a story for a long time without constant stimulation. And I think it develops empathy. When children read about characters from different backgrounds, they learn to see the world through other people's eyes. That's why I think parents should read with their kids from a very early age.

part3.q: Will printed books disappear in the future?
part3.sample: I don't think they'll disappear completely, at least not in the near future. E-books and audiobooks are definitely growing, because they're cheap and convenient. But many people still love the physical experience of a printed book, the feel of the paper, the smell and the satisfaction of putting a finished book on a shelf. Printed books also make much better gifts than e-books. I suspect paper books will become a bit like vinyl records, less common, but still treasured by a loyal group of readers.

part3.q: Should governments spend money on public libraries?
part3.sample: Yes, I strongly believe they should. Libraries give everyone free access to books and information, which is especially important for families who can't afford to buy many books. Modern libraries do much more than lend books, too. Many offer free Wi-Fi, quiet study spaces, computer classes for older people and activities for children. In my city, the main library is always full of students at weekends, because their homes are too small or noisy to study in. That shows how much they're still needed.

cueCard.title: Describe a documentary you watched that you found interesting.
points: when and where you watched it
cueCard.final: and explain why you found it interesting.

sample:
I'd like to talk about a nature documentary series about the deep ocean that I watched a few months ago. I can't remember the exact title, but it had six episodes, and I came across it on a streaming platform one evening when I was looking for something relaxing to watch.

I watched it at home over two weekends, mostly with my flatmate, and we got completely hooked. Each episode focused on a different part of the ocean, from coral reefs to the deepest trenches, which are more than ten kilometres down. The filming was incredible. The crew used special submarines and cameras that could cope with the enormous pressure and total darkness at those depths.

I learned a huge amount from it. For example, I had no idea that many deep-sea creatures can produce their own light, which they use to attract food or confuse predators. There was one fish with a glowing lure hanging in front of its mouth, like a fishing rod, which looked like something out of a science fiction film. I also learned that some ecosystems survive around hot volcanic vents on the sea floor without any sunlight at all.

The reason I found it so interesting is that it showed me a world I knew almost nothing about, even though it covers most of our planet. But the last episode was quite sobering. It showed plastic waste that had been found even in the deepest parts of the ocean, which really shocked me. Since then, I've made a real effort to cut down on single-use plastic, like takeaway containers.

part3.q: Why do some people prefer documentaries to other types of TV programmes?
part3.sample: I think people who enjoy documentaries like the feeling that they're learning something while they relax. After a long day, watching a reality show can feel like a waste of time, whereas a good documentary leaves you with new knowledge or a different perspective. Documentaries are also based on real events and real people, which can make them more powerful than fiction. When you know a story actually happened, it tends to have a stronger emotional impact.

part3.q: Can documentaries change people's behaviour?
part3.sample: I believe they can, at least to some extent. A powerful documentary can raise awareness of an issue that people had never really thought about. For example, after some well-known nature documentaries showed sea creatures harmed by plastic, there was a noticeable rise in public support for banning plastic straws and bags in several countries. However, the effect doesn't always last. People might feel strongly for a week and then go back to their old habits, unless there are practical changes, like new laws, to support them.

part3.q: Do you trust the information you see in documentaries?
part3.sample: Mostly, yes, but not completely. Documentaries made by well-known organisations usually check their facts carefully and interview real experts. However, every documentary is edited, and the filmmakers decide what to include and what to leave out, so they can still present a one-sided view. Some are even made to promote a particular product or political position. That's why I think it's a good idea to check who produced a documentary and, if the topic is controversial, look at other sources too.

part3.q: How has the way people watch TV changed in recent years?
part3.sample: It's changed enormously. Most people I know hardly ever watch traditional TV channels anymore. Instead, they use streaming platforms and video apps, so they can watch whatever they like, whenever they like, often on their phones. Binge-watching a whole series in one weekend has become completely normal. Another big change is the rise of short videos. Many young people now prefer clips that last just a minute or two, which some experts worry is shortening our attention spans.
